entry.title: Secure Your Cloud Integration iFlows with OAuth 2.0 Using SAP API Management
entry.content:
Imagine a third party needs to call your integration flow. You don't want to hand over your Cloud Integration service key. You'd rather give them a separate key and secret that you can control, revoke, and track per product.

SAP API Management in Integration Suite lets you do exactly that. In this blog, you'll build:

  1. A "Generate Token" proxy, which issues OAuth access tokens
  2. An iFlow proxy, which verifies those tokens before letting requests through
  3. A product and subscription, which provide the key and secret for consumers
  4. A test in Postman or Bruno, to see it all work

The Big Picture

Client (Postman/3rd party)
             │ 1. Key + Secret
            ▼
[Generate Token Proxy] ──► Access Token
           │
           │ 2. Call with Bearer Token
          ▼
[iFlow Proxy] ── Verify Token ──► Cloud Integration iFlow

 
Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have:

  • Access to SAP Integration Suite with the API Management capability enabled
  • A deployed iFlow that you want to expose
  • The service key of your Process Integration Runtime instance (plan: integration-flow). You'll need the client ID, client secret, and token URL.
  • Postman or Bruno for testing

Part 1: Create the "Generate Token" Proxy

This proxy is the endpoint your consumers will call to get an OAuth token.

Step 1: Create an API Provider 
  1. Open Integration Suite.
  2. Go to Configure → APIs → API Providers.
  3. Click Create.

     

  4. Enter a Name for your API Provider.


    Configure the connection

    Switch to the Connection tab and fill in the following:


    Field
    Value
    TypeCloud Integration
    HostThe host from the url in your service key (see tip below)
    Port443
    AuthenticationOAuth2ClientCredentials
    Client IDclientid from the service key
    Client Secretclientsecret from the service key
    Token URLtokenurl from the service key

    Tip:     Use the service key of your Process Integration Runtime instance with plan api. For the host, copy only the domain from the url field, without https:// and without any path.
    Then click Save.

 

Test the connection

Click Test Connection. If everything is set up correctly, you'll see a success message like this:

 

Your API Provider is ready! We'll use it later to expose your iFlow through an API proxy.

Step 2: Create the API Proxy

  1. Under Configure → APIs, click Create to create a new API proxy.
  2. Select URL as the source.
  3. Enter any placeholder URL. It must start with https:// and end with .com (for example, https://example.com).
  4. Give your proxy a Name and a Title.
  5. Enter a Base Path of your choice. It becomes part of your proxy endpoint URL.
  6. Click Create.
    Tip: The URL is only a placeholder. This proxy never calls it, because the OAuth policy that we add next responds to the request itself.

🎉Your proxy exists. Now we make it generate tokens.

Step 3: Add the OAuth v2.0 policy (GenerateAccessToken)
  1. Open your proxy and click Policies.

     

  2. Go to Proxy Endpoint → PreFlow in the left panel.
  3. On the right, find the OAuth v2.0 SET policy and click the + icon.
  4. Give the policy a name and click Add.
  5. Paste this XML:

<OAuthV2 async="false" continueOnError="false" enabled="true" xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <Operation>GenerateAccessToken</Operation>
    <GenerateResponse/>
    <SupportedGrantTypes>
        <GrantType>client_credentials</GrantType>
    </SupportedGrantTypes>
</OAuthV2>​

 


What does this policy do?
It generates and returns an OAuth access token for a client application using the client_credentials grant type. This grant type is the usual choice for system-to-system communication, where no end user logs in.
  1. Click Update → Save → Deploy.

Checkpoint: Copy the proxy endpoint URL. This is your Token URL, and you'll need it in the testing step.

Part 2: Create the Proxy for Your iFlow

Now we expose the actual iFlow and protect it.

Step 1: Before creating the iFlow proxy, you need the Cloud Integration API Provider that we created in Part 1 → Step 1. The proxy uses it to connect to your Cloud Integration tenant.
Step 2: Create the API Proxy from the Provider

This time, don't choose URL. Instead:

  1. Create a new API proxy and select Provider as the source.
  2. Choose the Cloud Integration provider you just created.
  3. Click Discover and select the iFlow you want to expose.
  4. Click Next.


Step 3: Configure authentication to the backend

On the next screen:

  • Authentication Type: OAuth2ClientCredentials
  • Client ID and Client Secret: from your Process Integration Runtime service key
  • Token URL: also from the service key

     

Don't mix these up!
The credentials here are the service key values (Plan - iflow), used by API Management to talk to Cloud Integration. Your consumers will later use a different key and secret, generated from the product subscription.

Step 4: Finalize the proxy details
  • Adjust the Base Path if you like. It appears in your endpoint URL.
  • Leave the other settings as they are.
  • Choose the Service Type that matches your iFlow's sender adapter (for example SOAP or REST).
  • Click Create.

     

🎉Your iFlow proxy is created.

Step 5: Add the OAuth v2.0 policy (VerifyAccessToken)
  1. Open Policies and add an OAuth v2.0 policy.
  2. Paste this XML:

<OAuthV2 async="false" continueOnError="true" enabled="true" xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <ExternalAuthorization>false</ExternalAuthorization>
    <Operation>VerifyAccessToken</Operation>
    <GenerateResponse enabled="true"/>
    <SupportedGrantTypes/>
    <Tokens/>
</OAuthV2>​

 


What does this policy do?
It verifies the access token sent by the client. If the token is valid, the request goes through. If not, an error response is returned. Place it on any protected API so that only authenticated clients get in.
  1. Click Update → Save → Deploy.

Checkpoint: You now have an endpoint URL for your iFlow proxy. Keep it handy.

Part 3: Bundle Everything into a Product

Consumers don't subscribe to individual proxies. They subscribe to products. So let's create one containing both proxies.

Step 1: Create the product
  1. Go to Engage → Products.
  2. Click Create.
  3. Enter a Name for the product.

Step 2: Add your proxies
  1. Open the APIs tab.
  2. Add both proxies:
    • ✔️The Generate Token proxy
    • ✔️The iFlow proxy

Why both?
Consumers need one to get the token and the other to use it. If either is missing from the product, the flow breaks.

Step 3: Publish

Click Publish to make the product available.

Part 4: Subscribe in the Developer Hub

Step 1: Open the Developer Hub

Step 2: Find your product and subscribe
  1. Search for your product and open it.

     

  2. From the Subscribe dropdown, select New subscription for application.

     

  3. Give the subscription a name and click Create.

     

Step 3: Grab your credentials 

After the subscription is created, you'll see a Key and a Secret.

  • They act as your Client ID and Client Secret for OAuth 2.0.
  • You can share them with third parties.
  • Every product subscription gets its own key and secret, so you can manage each consumer separately.

Part 5: Test It in Postman or Bruno 

Step 1: Set up the request
  1. Create a new request with the iFlow proxy endpoint URL.
  2. Under Auth, choose OAuth 2.0.
  3. Set Grant Type to Client Credentials.

Step 2: Fill in the token details

 

Field
Value
Access Token URLThe URL of your Generate Token proxy (Part 1)
Client IDKey from the Developer Hub
Client SecretSecret from the Developer Hub

Step 3: Generate the token and send the request
  1. Click Get / Generate Access Token.
  2. Use the token in your request.
  3. Send the request to your iFlow proxy endpoint.

🎉Success!

Quick Recap
  1. ✅Created a Generate Token proxy with the GenerateAccessToken policy
  2. ✅Created an iFlow proxy with the VerifyAccessToken policy
  3. ✅Bundled both into a product and published it
  4. ✅Subscribed in the Developer Hub to get a key and secret
  5. ✅Tested the flow in Postman or Bruno
Over to you!

Did this setup work for you? Are you using OAuth 2.0 for other scenarios, such as different grant types or custom scopes? Share your experience or questions in the comments below. I'd love to hear how you're securing your APIs.

If you found this helpful, give it a 👍 and follow me for more SAP Integration Suite content.

entry.title: Handling Job Approval Rejection in SAP SmartRecruiters: Re-triggering Approvals via API
entry.content:
When Does SmartRecruiters Re-trigger Approval Automatically?

Before building an integration, it is important to understand the native behaviour. A re-approval is triggered automatically when any of the following position fields are updated:

  • Position Open Date
  • Target Start Date
  • Position Type
  • Position ID
  • Salary Range (min, max, currency)
Key Limitation: If an approver rejects the job asking for a change to a field not in the list above — such as job location, job advertisement text, or a custom job field — the system will not automatically re-trigger the approval after the update. An API-based integration is required.

The Integration Approach

The solution consists of four steps, all orchestrated by listening to a single webhook event fired by SmartRecruiters:

 

 

  Step 1    Detect the Rejection via Webhook

Configure the job.approval.step.rejected webhook event in SmartRecruiters. This event fires the moment any approval step is rejected, delivering the jobId and approval context to your integration endpoint.

 

Step 2    Retrieve the Approval ID

Use the job's ID (received from the webhook payload) to fetch the latest approval record. This call returns the approvalRequestId which is required for all further operations on that approval.

GET    https://api.smartrecruiters.com/jobs/{jobId}/approvals/latest

Example call:

https://api.smartrecruiters.com/jobs/33b57035-317d-4b4a-aa30-44d2e8cc928f/approvals/latest

 

 

  Step 3    Read the Rejection Reason (Optional but Recommended)

Before creating a new approval, fetch the approver's rejection comment. This allows your integration to log the reason, notify the recruiter, or route the notification differently based on the rejection message.

  GET    https://api.smartrecruiters.com/approvals-api/v201910/approvals/{approvalId}/comments

Example call:

https://api.smartrecruiters.com/approvals-api/v201910/approvals/801e28f7-e212-4859-9908-2935d0d25b37/comments

  Step 4    Create a New Approval

After the recruiter has made the requested changes, trigger a fresh approval by posting to the Approvals API. The key field is baseId — set it to the approvalRequestId retrieved in Step 2. This links the new approval to the original job context.

  POST    https://api.smartrecruiters.com/approvals-api/v201910/approvals

Request body:

{
  "baseId": "801e28f7-e212-4859-9908-2935d0d25b37",
  "type": "sequential",
  "decisionMode": "any",
  "steps": [
    {
      "approvers": [
        { "id": "6a986436be2958fa852dda78" }
      ]
    },
    {
      "approvers": [
        { "id": "6a98643697a14f8c43c2a454" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Response (201 Created):

"id": "f96a769b-788a-4fab-b1b3-bc9bacefba76",
    "subject": {
        "id": "33b57035-317d-4b4a-aa30-44d2e8cc928f",
        "type": "job"
    },
    "status": "PENDING",
    "type": "sequential",
    "decisionMode": "any",
    "steps": [
        {
            "status": "PENDING",
            "approvers": [
                {
                    "id": "6a986436be2958fa852dda78",
                    "decision": "PENDING"
                }
            ]
        },
        {
            "status": "PENDING",
            "approvers": [
                {
                    "id": "6a98643697a14f8c43c2a454",
                    "decision": "PENDING"
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}

  • baseId: The approvalRequestId of the original (rejected) approval. Mandatory for re-approval.
  • type: sequential — approvers are notified one after another in order.
  • decisionMode: any — approval is granted once any approver in a step approves.
  • steps: An ordered array of approval steps, each containing one or more approver user IDs.

Verifying the Result in SmartRecruiters UI

After the API call succeeds, the job transitions through two visible states in the SmartRecruiters interface:

Before — Approval Rejected

 


 

After — New Approval Pending

 

Summary

When a job approval is rejected in SmartRecruiters for reasons that do not automatically re-trigger the native re-approval flow, the Approvals API provides a clean programmatic path to restart the process. The end-to-end integration pattern is:

  1. Subscribe to the job.approval.step.rejected webhook event.
  2. Call GET /jobs/{jobId}/approvals/latest to retrieve the approvalRequestId.
  3. Optionally call GET /approvals-api/v201910/approvals/{approvalId}/comments to capture the rejection reason.
  4. After the recruiter makes the necessary updates, call POST /approvals-api/v201910/approvals with baseId set to the original approval ID to create a fresh approval chain.

 

This approach gives integration teams full control over the re-approval lifecycle, ensures no job falls through the cracks after a rejection, and provides a complete audit trail of rejection reasons and re-submission history.

Thanks

Kunal

entry.title: When AI Meets SAP Integration: Exploring the New Possibilities of API Management
entry.content:
Imagine asking an AI assistant a simple business question:

“Can you check where my order is and tell me whether it will arrive tomorrow?”

For a person, this sounds like a straightforward request. But behind that one question, several things might need to happen. The assistant may need to retrieve the order from SAP, check delivery information, contact a logistics service, and combine the results before responding.

For an enterprise, this is where things get interesting.

The challenge is no longer just connecting one system to another. It is making business capabilities available to AI applications without losing control over security, access, and governance.

This is one of the areas where SAP Integration Suite is evolving, particularly through API Management, API-centric integration, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) support.

As someone working with SAP integration scenarios, I find this an interesting direction because it raises a practical question: How can we make the APIs and integration capabilities enterprises already have useful to AI applications?

From connecting systems to enabling AI

For years, integration development has focused on connecting applications, transforming payloads, routing messages, and ensuring that business data reaches the right destination.

A typical integration might retrieve a file from SFTP, transform CSV data into XML, and deliver the result to an SAP-related system. Another might expose an API that retrieves customer or delivery information.

These patterns remain important. But when an AI assistant enters the picture, there is another requirement: the assistant needs a structured and controlled way to discover and use the capabilities that already exist.

An AI agent should not simply have unrestricted access to every backend system. It needs access to the right operations, with appropriate permissions and safeguards.

This is where API Management becomes more than a place to manage API traffic. It can help establish the controls around how enterprise capabilities are exposed and consumed.

Where does MCP fit into this picture?

One concept worth understanding is the Model Context Protocol, or MCP.

MCP provides a standardized way for compatible AI applications to discover and interact with tools and resources. Instead of building a separate, custom connection for every AI application and every backend capability, developers can expose selected operations through an MCP-compatible interface.

Let's return to our delivery-status example.

The organization already has an API that retrieves delivery information. It may also have an API that retrieves order details. The business logic does not necessarily need to be rebuilt just because an AI assistant is introduced.

Instead, selected capabilities can be made available to an AI agent through a suitable MCP-based architecture.

The agent can discover an available tool, provide the required input, and use the returned result to answer the user's question.

MCP does not replace the underlying APIs. It provides a standardized way for AI applications to interact with capabilities exposed through compatible MCP servers.

Bringing the pieces together

This is where SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway becomes relevant. It provides a way to govern access to MCP-based capabilities, helping connect AI consumers with enterprise services through a managed entry point.

Consider the following conceptual architecture.

                  Business User
                       |
                       v
                 AI Assistant
                       |
                       v
                    MCP Client
                       |
                       v
              +--------------------+
              | SAP Integration    |
              | Suite              |
              |                    |
              |     MCP Gateway    |
              |                    |
              | Authentication     |
              | Access Governance  |
              | Traffic Controls   |
              +--------------------+
                       |
                 +-----+-----+
                 |           |
                 v           v
           SAP Business   Logistics
                API          API
                 |           |
                 v           v
             SAP S/4HANA   Tracking System
                 |           |
                 +-----+-----+
                       |
                       v
             Delivery Information
                       |
                       v
                 AI Assistant
                       |
                       v
             Response to the User

Figure: A conceptual architecture showing how an AI assistant could access selected SAP and third-party business capabilities through a governed MCP entry point.

The important point is not the number of components in the diagram. It is the separation of responsibilities.

The business APIs continue to provide the underlying operations. The MCP interface enables compatible AI applications to discover and invoke selected tools. The gateway provides a place to apply appropriate governance and traffic controls.

This is particularly useful to consider in enterprise landscapes, where one business process can span multiple applications, APIs, and security boundaries.

The exact architecture will depend on the available services, the MCP client, authentication requirements, and the capabilities supported by the organization's SAP Integration Suite environment.

API Management is also getting smarter

The AI story does not stop at exposing APIs to AI agents. AI can also help developers and administrators understand the APIs they already manage.

SAP API Management provides an AI-assisted analytics experience that allows users to explore API usage and performance through natural-language questions.

Think about a developer investigating an API that has suddenly started receiving more requests than usual. Rather than beginning with several filters and dashboard views, the developer could use a natural-language question to explore the available analytics.

Questions about request volumes, API performance, or consumer activity can become a more accessible starting point for investigation.

The generated insights still need to be checked against the underlying data, but this approach can make API analytics easier to explore.

For integration teams, that is an interesting shift: AI can become both a consumer of governed enterprise services and an assistant for people managing those services.

What is changing in SAP's integration landscape?

SAP's direction combines several related ideas.

API-centric integration brings API design, mediation, and governance closer together. MCP Gateway addresses the need to govern access to capabilities used by compatible AI applications. AI-assisted API analytics helps users explore API activity more naturally.

These capabilities solve different problems, but they point toward a common goal: making enterprise integration assets easier to expose, understand, and consume.

SAP's MCP support is also evolving. Its October 2026 release documentation describes support for MCP specification version 2026-07-28 and an increase in the maximum number of tools configurable on a single MCP server from 30 to 50.

These details matter when designing an implementation, but the bigger story is how standardized AI-to-tool communication can fit into an enterprise integration strategy.

As always, actual availability depends on the service, region, and tenant configuration, so the relevant SAP documentation should be checked before adopting a feature.

What does this mean for integration developers?

For developers who already work with SAP Cloud Integration, this is an extension of the integration landscape rather than a reason to abandon existing skills.

Payload transformation, connectivity, orchestration, security, and error handling remain fundamental. What changes is how some of the capabilities built on top of these foundations may be discovered and consumed.

An integration flow that retrieves or transforms business information may remain part of the solution. An API may provide access to that information. An MCP-based interface can then make a selected capability available to a compatible AI agent, with governance applied at the appropriate points.

Of course, not every integration needs AI. A scheduled file transfer or a straightforward system-to-system interface should not automatically become an AI use case.

The opportunity is to identify scenarios where natural-language interaction or agent-driven tool use adds real value, then expose only the capabilities needed for that scenario.

For me, that is the most useful way to think about these developments: the goal is not to add AI to every integration, but to make the right enterprise capabilities safely accessible when AI can genuinely help.

Closing thoughts

Enterprise integration is moving beyond the question of how systems exchange data. It is also becoming a question of how applications, people, and AI agents can access business capabilities in a controlled and meaningful way.

SAP Integration Suite's API Management developments, together with MCP support and AI-assisted analytics, are worth watching as this landscape evolves.

The underlying principles remain familiar: build clear interfaces, protect business data, govern access, and monitor how services are used. What is changing is the range of consumers that can make use of those services.

As AI becomes more integrated into enterprise workflows, the role of integration developers will continue to matter—not just in connecting systems, but in helping ensure that the capabilities behind those systems can be used responsibly.

entry.title: Scalable and Reliable Large-Volume Data Synchronization Using SAP Integration Suite Pipeline Orchest
entry.content:
Introduction

Organisations frequently need to synchronise large volumes of business data, such as master data, transactional records, financial information, and order data, between enterprise systems. Such integrations must be designed to process high data volumes efficiently while ensuring reliability, recover-ability, and minimal impact on source and target system performance.

This article describes an orchestration-based synchronisation framework built using SAP Integration Suite. The solution leverages JMS queues, pipeline integration flows, and parallel processing principles to transfer large datasets reliably and efficiently between source and target systems.

In this use case, the source system contains master data records that need to be synchronised with a target system without impacting operational performance.

The source system exposes APIs that provide the following capabilities:

  1. Retrieve the total number of records available for synchronisation.
  2. Retrieve a specific set of records based on page number and page size for a given date range.

By utilising SAP Integration Suite as the orchestration layer, large datasets can be split into manageable batches and processed independently, enabling scalability, fault tolerance, and efficient resource utilisation.

High-Level Solution Architecture

Process Flow Overview

  1. Initiation: Scheduled Trigger

The synchronisation process begins with a scheduler that triggers the workflow at predefined intervals based on business requirements.

Once triggered, a message is placed into an initial JMS queue. This design provides decoupling between process stages and ensures message persistence. In the event of temporary connectivity failures or unexpected processing issues, the message remains available for automatic retry and reprocessing.

Key Benefits

  • Scheduled execution
  • Reliable message persistence
  • Automatic recovery from transient failures
  • Decoupled processing architecture

  1. Planning: Determine Processing Scope and Create Jobs

After the workflow is initiated, the planning phase identifies the volume of data that must be synchronised.

During this step:

  • The source system API is invoked to retrieve the total record count.
  • The total number of pages is calculated based on the configured page size.
  • Required processing parameters are generated, including page number and page size.
  • A separate job message is created for each page of records.
  • All generated jobs are placed into a JMS queue for execution.

This approach converts a large synchronisation activity into multiple smaller and independently executable jobs.

Example

If:

  • Total Records = 1,000,000
  • Page Size = 10,000

Then:

  • Total Jobs = 100

Each job is responsible for processing one page of records.

Key Benefits

  • Workload distribution
  • Improved scalability
  • Independent processing of batches
  • Better system resource management 

  1. Execute Jobs from the Queue

Once jobs are available in the JMS queue, the execution flow starts processing them immediately.

For each job:

  • The corresponding message is consumed from the JMS queue.
  • The source API is called using the assigned page number and page size.
  • The requested batch of records is retrieved.

Using JMS as the processing backbone provides resilience against temporary API failures. If connectivity issues occur during execution, the message remains available for retry according to the configured retry mechanism.

Key Benefits

  • Reliable batch processing
  • Automatic retries
  • Failure isolation
  • Parallel execution capability

  1. Retrieve Records and Deliver to the Target System

After successfully retrieving a batch of records from the source system, the data is forwarded to the target system through the SAP Integration Suite pipeline framework.

The processing utilises:

  • Pipeline Generic Step 06 – Outbound Processing
  • Pipeline Generic Step 08 – XI Outbound Processing

Step 06 provides built-in retry capabilities and reliability handling. If message delivery fails during Step 08 processing, the framework automatically retries transmission based on the configured retry settings.

This layered design ensures guaranteed delivery while maintaining high throughput for large volumes of data.

Key Benefits

  • Reliable target system delivery
  • Automatic retry handling
  • Reduced data loss risk
  • Standardised outbound processing framework

Solution Benefits

The proposed orchestration pattern provides several advantages for enterprise-scale integrations:

Scalability

Large datasets are divided into smaller processing units, enabling efficient handling of millions of records.

Performance Optimisation

Paginated data retrieval minimises load on the source system while reducing memory consumption within the integration platform.

Reliability

JMS-based processing ensures message persistence and recovery from temporary failures.

Parallel Processing

Multiple jobs can be processed simultaneously, significantly reducing overall synchronisation time.

Re-usability

The framework can be reused for synchronising:

  • Master Data
  • Order Data
  • Financial Data
  • Customer Data
  • Product Data
  • Transactional Records

Monitoring and Support

Each job represents an individual processing unit, simplifying operational monitoring, troubleshooting, and error recovery.

Conclusion

By combining SAP Integration Suite Pipeline Flows, JMS queues, and pagination-based processing, organisations can build a scale able and resilient synchronisation framework capable of handling high-volume data transfers efficiently. The solution minimises dependency on source system performance, provides built-in recovery mechanisms, supports parallel processing, and ensures reliable delivery to downstream applications.

This orchestration pattern serves as a reusable enterprise integration blueprint for synchronising large-scale master data, transactional data, financial records, and other business-critical information across heterogeneous systems.

entry.title: Protect Your iFlows: Add Access Control, OAuth 2.0, Spike Arrest and Quota with SAP API Management
entry.content:
The Scenario

I have an integration flow like this:
3rd Party ──► CPI (iFlow) ──► SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud

It works, but the third party calls CPI directly. That raises a few questions:

  • What if they send thousands of requests in a second?
  • What if someone calls from an unknown IP?
  • How do I give them their own credentials without sharing my CPI service key?
  • How do I limit how much they can use?

The answer is an API Management layer in front of CPI:
3rd Party ──► API Management ──► CPI (iFlow) ──► SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud
                                (policies here)

In this blog, I'll show you how to build it, step by step.

 What You'll Build
  • An API Provider that connects API Management to Cloud Integration
  • An API Proxy for your iFlow
  • Four policies: Access Control, OAuth 2.0, Spike Arrest, Quota
  • An API Product with a subscription (key and secret)
  • A working test in Postman or Bruno
Prerequisites
  • SAP Integration Suite with API Management enabled
  • A deployed iFlow (mine uses an HTTP sender adapter)
  • Two service keys in BTP. This is where people often get confused:

 

Service instance plan
Used for
apiCreating the API Provider (Step 1)
integration-flowThe proxy's backend authentication to trigger the iFlow (Step 2)

Important: For the API Provider, create the instance with plan api, not the iFlow plan. Then create a service key for it.

Step 1: Create the API Provider (Cloud Integration)

The API Provider tells API Management where your Cloud Integration tenant lives and how to authenticate against it.

  1. Open Integration Suite.
  2. Go to Configure → APIs → API Providers and click Create.

     

  3. Give your API Provider a Name.

     

  4. Go to the Connection tab and fill in:
Field
Value
TypeCloud Integration
HostHost from the url in your api plan service key
Port443
AuthenticationOAuth2ClientCredentials
Client ID / Client Secret / Token URLFrom the same api plan service key

Click Save.

Click Test Connection. You should see a success message.

🎉Your API Provider is ready!

Step 2: Create the API Proxy for Your iFlow
  1. In the same window, go to API Proxies and click Create.

Select Provider as the source and choose the API Provider you just created.
Click Discover.


Choose your iFlow from the list and click Next.

 

Set the backend Authentication Type to OAuth2ClientCredentials, then enter:

  • Client ID and Client Secret from the integration-flow plan service key
  • Token URL from the same service key

If Basic Authentication works better for you, you can use that instead. Then click Done.

  1. Adjust the Base Path if you like, since it becomes part of your endpoint.
  2. Choose the Service Type that matches your iFlow's sender adapter (in my case, HTTP).
  3. Leave everything else as is and click Create.

🎉Your API Proxy is created. Now let's make it smart.

Step 3: Meet the Policies

I'll apply four policies. Here's what each one does:

Policy
What it does
Think of it as
Access ControlAllows or denies requests based on the caller's IP addressA security guard checking the guest list
OAuth 2.0Verifies that the caller sends a valid access tokenAn ID badge check
Spike ArrestProtects the backend from sudden bursts of traffic by limiting the request rateA speed limiter
QuotaLimits the total number of calls a consumer can make in a time periodA monthly data plan

Spike Arrest vs. Quota: Spike Arrest protects APIs from sudden traffic spikes by smoothing short-term bursts (typically requests per second). Quota controls the total number of requests a consumer can make over a longer period (such as per hour, day, or month). Both policies complement each other and are often used together to provide effective traffic management.

How to open the policy editor
  1. Open your API Proxy and click Policies.

     

  2. Go to Proxy Endpoint → PreFlow in the left panel.
  3. On the right, you'll see the available policies. Find the one you need and click +.
  4. Give the policy a name and click Add.

You can reorder policies using the arrows in the upper right. I recommend this order: Access Control → OAuth 2.0 → Spike Arrest → Quota. Cheap checks go first, so bad traffic is rejected early.

 Policy 1: OAuth 2.0

Find OAuth v2.0 in the list, click +, name it, and click Add.

To use OAuth Policy, you also need a separate API proxy that generates the access token.

👉I've covered this in a separate blog: [link]. Please follow it first, then come back here.

Policy 2: Access Control

Find Access Control in the list, click +, and apply this policy:

 
<AccessControl xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt" async="true" continueOnError="false" enabled="true">
    <IPRules noRuleMatchAction="DENY">
        <MatchRule action="ALLOW">
            <!-- Load Balancer -->
            <SourceAddress mask="32">Paste IP Here</SourceAddress>
            <!-- App Servers -->
            <SourceAddress mask="32">Paste IP Here</SourceAddress>
        </MatchRule>
    </IPRules>
</AccessControl>​



How it works: Any IP not on the allow list is denied (noRuleMatchAction="DENY"). Replace the placeholders with your third party's real IPs.
Make sure enabled="true". With enabled="false", the policy exists but does nothing.
Which mask should I use?

The mask defines how many IPs a rule covers. Here is a cheat sheet.

Mask
Subnet mask
IPs covered
Example
Typical use
32255.255.255.2551203.0.113.25 onlyA single server, such as a third party's fixed IP. Best for most cases.
31255.255.255.2542.24 to .25Two paired servers
30255.255.255.2524.24 to .27A small group of servers
29255.255.255.2488.24 to .31A small server group
28255.255.255.24016.16 to .31A small office or datacenter block
27255.255.255.22432.0 to .31A medium block
26255.255.255.19264.0 to .63A larger block
25255.255.255.128128.0 to .127Half of a /24 network
24255.255.255.0256.0 to .255A whole company subnet
16255.255.0.065,536203.0.0.0 to 203.0.255.255A very large network. Usually too wide.
8255.0.0.016,777,216203.0.0.0 to 203.255.255.255Huge. Almost never appropriate.
00.0.0.0All IPsEverythingMatches everyone, so the rule becomes meaningless.
 Policy 3: Spike Arrest

Find Spike Arrest, click +, give it a name, and click Add.


<SpikeArrest async="true" continueOnError="false" enabled="true" xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <Identifier ref="request.header.some-header-name"/>
    <MessageWeight ref="request.header.weight"/>
    <Rate>100ps</Rate>
    <UseEffectiveCount>true</UseEffectiveCount>
</SpikeArrest>

 

In plain words: This policy limits traffic to 100 requests per second per unique header value. The request's weight can reduce the allowed number further. This helps prevent backend overload and keeps your API stable.
Policy 4: Quota

Find Quota, click +, give it a name, and click Add.

<Quota async="false" continueOnError="false" enabled="true" type="calendar" xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <Allow count="1000"/>
    <Interval>5</Interval>
    <Distributed>true</Distributed>
    <StartTime>2026-10-16 05:26:00</StartTime>
    <Synchronous>true</Synchronous>
    <TimeUnit>minute</TimeUnit>
</Quota>

In plain words: API consumers can make a maximum of 1000 calls in every 5-minute period.
Set StartTime to the current date and time, or a past one, so the counter starts immediately.
Save and Deploy

Click Update → Save → Deploy.

You now have a wrapper endpoint that you can share with third parties. 🎉
At this stage, you could already share the api plan service key credentials. But there's a cleaner, more professional way: API Products.

Step 4: Create an API Product

Products let you give each consumer their own key and secret, instead of sharing your service key.

  1. Go to Engage → Products and click Create.

     

  2. Enter a Name.
  3. Open the APIs tab and add the API proxies we created:
    • ✔️Your iFlow proxy
    • ✔️The Generate Token proxy (from the OAuth blog)

       

Click Publish.

Step 5: Subscribe in the Developer Hub
  1. Open the Developer Hub.

  1. Find your product and open it.

     

  2. From the Subscribe dropdown, select New subscription for application.

     

  3. Give the subscription a name and click Create.


You'll now see a Key and a Secret 🔑


You can give these to your third parties. Every product subscription gets its own credentials, so you can manage each consumer separately.

Using only an API key?
You can share just the key and ask the consumer to send it in the header as x-api-key. This works when you're using API key / Basic Authentication, and you may need to add a matching policy such as Verify API Key or Basic Authentication.

Since I'm using OAuth 2.0, the key and secret act as Client ID and Client Secret instead. Let's test that.

Step 6: Test with Postman / Bruno
  1. Create a new request with the API proxy endpoint URL of your iFlow.
  2. Under Auth, choose OAuth 2.0 and set Grant Type to Client Credentials.

Fill in the token details:

 

Field
Value
Access Token URLURL of the Generate Token proxy (see my OAuth blog: [link])
Client IDKey from the Developer Hub
Client SecretSecret from the Developer Hub

Click Generate Token, then use it to call your iFlow through the same API Management endpoint.

🎉Success!

Recap
  1. ✅Created an API Provider (api plan key)
  2. ✅Created an API Proxy for the iFlow (integration-flow plan key)
  3. ✅Applied OAuth 2.0, Access Control, Spike Arrest, and Quota
  4. ✅Bundled everything into a Product and subscribed
  5. ✅Tested with OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials
Over to You

Which policies do you use most in your projects? Have you tried others, such as JSON threat protection or response caching? Let me know in the comments!

If this helped you, give it a 👍 and follow for more SAP Integration Suite content.

entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 6: Transporting destinations
entry.content:
Part 6 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 5 role collections travelled through the Content Agent UI and needed an extra role and their own destination. Destinations are the opposite: they use the same road as integration packages and need almost no setup. The one thing to remember is what stays behind.

What travels and what stays behind

SAP's list of supported content types includes SAP Destination Service with the sub type Destination, and adds a clear note: "Content Agent service does not transport secrets and passwords." So the destination arrives in Central, but you enter its password or client secret there again yourself.

For the setup column, the same page says No setup needed. No new destination, no new node, no new route.

Step 1: Check the content type in Dev

Open the Content Agent UI in Dev and go to Content Types. SAP Destination Service should show Active. In my setup it already was.

Step 2: Pick the destination

Choose Export. On Add Content, search for the destination name and select the row with type Destination Service and sub type Destination.

Add Content in my setup: a role collection and a destination with the same name. The Type column tells them apart.

Step 3: Export to CTMS

On Export Details, the same choices as in Part 5: Export Mode SAP Cloud Transport Management, Create a New Transport Request, the source node and a description. I left Keep this Transport Request modifiable unchecked. Then Review and Export.

The log is worth a quick read: the MTAR is created, the request is created as not modifiable, and the last line confirms the content was transported to CTMS.

Export log in my setup (node name and process ID blurred).

Step 4: Import in Central

In CTMS, open the target node from Part 3, the one that uses CAS_on_target. The request lands in the same import queue as your integration packages. Select it, choose Import and confirm. In my setup the status changed to Succeeded.

Step 5: Finish the destination

  • In Central, go to Connectivity > Destinations. The destination is in the list.
  • Open it, enter the password or client secret again and save.
  • Test it from the application that uses it. For OAuth2ClientCredentials destinations, SAP Help notes that Check Connection is not a reliable test.

What tripped me up in my setup

  • Two items with the same name. When I searched on Add Content, a role collection and a destination were both called "Test". Only the Type column showed which was which. Give destinations names you can recognise, and always check the type before you export.
  • Other requests were waiting in the queue. The target node already had older requests in status Initial. I selected only the destination request. CTMS then warned that importing single requests can lead to inconsistencies, because it does not check dependencies between requests. A destination on its own is fine. If an iFlow depends on it, import the destination first or together with the package.
  • No extra role this time. After Part 5 I expected another role problem. There was none: the destination import worked through the existing setup from Parts 3 and 4.

What comes next

Packages, role collections and destinations now all travel from Dev to Central. In Part 7, the last part, I put the whole series on one page: every service, destination and role in a single cheat sheet.

But just to set the stage: what is SAP Managed File Transfer, and why should you consider it?

File transfer - a stubborn gap in enterprise integration

Large files, strict audit requirements and external partners still make file transfer one of the most stubborn gaps in enterprise integration – and often the one that holds up an S/4HANA go-live.

Because APIs and events get most of the attention in integration conversations. Yet in almost every SAP landscape, a surprisingly large share of business-critical data still moves as files: such as payment and bank statement files, EDI documents with suppliers and customers, payroll exports, product and pricing catalogs, regulatory submissions and batch extracts for analytics.

And these requirements are hard to manage properly:

  • Size and volume. Multi-gigabyte files and high-volume batch runs push message-based integration platforms beyond what they're designed for.
  • Compliance. Regulations such as SOX, HIPAA, GDPR and PCI-DSS require encryption, complete audit trails and defined retention – evidence that ad-hoc FTP servers and scripts rarely provide.
  • External partners. Banks, suppliers, logistics providers and authorities each bring their own protocols, keys and schedules. Onboarding every new partner often means another IT ticket, another script and another server nobody wants to own.

In many companies, the result is a patchwork of legacy SFTP servers, scheduled jobs and custom code, with little visibility into what was sent, when and to whom. And this patchwork tends to surface at the worst possible moment: during an S/4HANA transformation. When teams inventory their interfaces, file-based flows often turn out to be the largest and least-documented group – and with SAP Process Orchestration approaching the end of mainstream maintenance, they need a future-proof home.

SAP Managed File Transfer by Redwood closes that gap

As an SAP Solution Extension – co-sold, co-developed and co-supported by SAP – SAP Managed File Transfer (MFT) by Redwood handles what general-purpose integration platforms aren't built for: multi-gigabyte files, audit retention for SOX, HIPAA, GDPR and PCI-DSS, and partner self-service exchanges that don't need IT for every transfer.

Combined with SAP Integration Suite, it covers your full integration architecture under a single SAP relationship.
